title: Older drivers in New York: renewal, vision tests and the keys talk
seoTitle: Older Drivers in NY: License Renewal and Safety Rules
seoDesc: New York has no age-based road test. How license renewal and the vision test work, how families can ask the DMV for a review, and the 10% insurance course.
dek: New York never ends a license because of age. Here is how renewal and the vision test work, how a family member can ask the DMV to review a driver, and how to plan for life after driving.
keyFacts: No age-based road test; DMV acts only on driving ability
Licenses last 8 years; renew 1 year early to 2 years late
Vision test at every renewal: at least 20/40, glasses allowed
Families use form DS-7, mailed to the DMV Medical Review Unit
Defensive driving course: 10% off base insurance rate for 3 years
body:
New York does not take away a driver's license because of age, and there is no automatic road test at any birthday. Every driver renews every eight years and must pass a vision test, with at least 20/40 vision in one or both eyes, with or without glasses.

If a family member or doctor is worried, they can ask the DMV in writing to re-evaluate the driver, and the DMV will decide based on driving ability. This guide covers renewal and the vision rule, how a review request works, the defensive driving insurance discount, warning signs, and other ways to get around once the keys are put away.

Does New York require older drivers to retest?

No. The DMV says it will not remove driving privileges based on age, or on any standard except driving ability. There is no age at which a road test or written test is required just for renewal.

What New York does require of every driver at renewal is a vision test. The DMV can also require a re-evaluation of any driver, of any age, when it has "reasonable grounds" to believe the person is not qualified to drive. Under the DMV's rules, that means a specific reason tied to driving, such as an incident or behavior reported by a doctor, a police officer or someone who knows or has observed the driver.

The DMV also runs a crash re-examination program for drivers of all ages who have three or more reportable crashes within 18 months. Those drivers are called in for an interview and possible eye, written and road tests.

In New York, age alone never ends a license. Ability does.

How do you renew a license in New York?

A New York driver license is valid for eight years. You can renew online, by mail or at a DMV office, from one year before it expires to two years after.

RuleWhat the DMV says
How long a license lasts8 years
Renewal windowUp to 1 year before and 2 years after expiration
Vision standardAt least 20/40 in either or both eyes, with or without corrective lenses
Vision result good for12 months (an eye doctor may set 6 months)
Class D renewal fee$64.50, or $80.50 in the MCTD counties (the five boroughs, Dutchess, Nassau, Orange, Putnam, Rockland, Suffolk and Westchester)
Expired 2 years or moreMust apply as a new driver, with written test, pre-licensing course and road test

How does the vision test work?

Your parent can take the vision test at a DMV office, or have it done by a provider. Providers enrolled in the DMV Online Vision Registry send results electronically, so the renewal can be done online without entering test details. Your parent can also have a physician, physician assistant, ophthalmologist, optometrist, optician, registered nurse or nurse professional fill out a Vision Test Report (MV-619). Find enrolled providers with the DMV's Vision Registry Locator by ZIP code.

If glasses are needed to pass, a "B" (corrective lenses) restriction goes on the license. If an eye care professional reports that night vision is impaired, the DMV adds a "Daylight driving only" restriction.

  1. Check the date. Look at the expiration date on the license and watch for the DMV renewal notice in the mail.
  2. Get the vision test. Use a Vision Registry provider, or have a qualified professional complete form MV-619. Results are good for 12 months.
  3. Pick how to renew. Renew online through the DMV or MyDMV, or mail the renewal notice, vision report and a check payable to "Commissioner of Motor Vehicles" to NYS DMV, 207 Genesee Street, Suite 6, Utica, NY 13501-2874.
  4. Go in person if needed. An office visit is required to switch to a REAL ID or Enhanced license, update the photo or change license class.
  5. Print the temporary license. After renewing online, you can print a temporary license that is valid for 60 days.

Driving on an expired license is costly. The DMV lists fines of $25 to $40 if it has been 60 days or less, and $75 to $300 after that, plus surcharges.

How can a family member report an unsafe driver to the DMV?

A family member, neighbor or friend uses form DS-7, Request for Driver Review, and mails the signed original to the DMV's Medical Review Unit. The DMV does not accept these requests by phone or email.

The form asks for the driver's name, address and date of birth, your name, address, phone and relationship, and specific incidents with dates and places. You can list other people who agree. The DMV will not act unless all four parts are complete, and it must include your name and signature. The form warns that the review may lead to suspension or revocation.

Mail it to: Medical Review Unit, NYS DMV, 6 Empire State Plaza, Room 337, Albany, NY 12228.

What happens after a report?

  • A DMV license examiner where the driver lives reviews the form. If there is a valid reason, the driver gets a certified letter to come in for an interview.
  • A vision test is required. The letter may also ask the driver to bring a Physician's Statement (MV-80), a registered and inspected car, and a licensed driver.
  • At the interview, the examiner explains what was reported and lets the driver respond. The examiner can require a written test and a road test.
  • If the driver doesn't show up, the license is suspended until they appear. If they fail the vision or written test, it is suspended until they pass.
  • If the driver fails the road test, the license is revoked. The driver can reapply after at least 30 days.

The DMV says that when a report comes from someone other than a physician, it considers each case separately and does not act without first re-evaluating the driver.

Can a doctor report a driver?

Yes. Doctors use form DS-6, and police use form DS-5. The DMV notes that New York law does not require doctors to report impaired drivers. If a physician reports a condition that affects driving, the DMV can suspend the license until a physician certifies the condition is treated or controlled.

What is the defensive driving insurance discount?

New York's Point and Insurance Reduction Program (PIRP), also called the defensive driving course, cuts the base rate of auto insurance premiums by 10% each year for three years. It can also reduce up to 4 points when calculating a suspension.

Courses are offered by private companies and organizations approved by the DMV, in a classroom, online or by other methods. The classroom version runs 320 minutes, and there is no test. Fees vary by provider. A few rules from the DMV:

  • Take it once every 36 months to keep the insurance discount.
  • Only the principal operator on a policy gets the 10% reduction.
  • Give the certificate to the insurer within 90 days so the discount starts from the course date.
  • Points don't come off the record. Four are subtracted only for figuring a suspension.

The DMV also points older drivers to courses such as the AARP Driver Safety Program, AAA's Safe Driving for Mature Operators and the National Safety Council's Coaching the Mature Driver. It suggests asking your insurer whether it offers a discount for older driver classes.

What are the warning signs it may be time to stop?

The DMV lists signs that driving skills are slipping. It says to be concerned if a driver:

  • has a number of minor crashes or near misses
  • can't concentrate, or has wandering thoughts
  • can't easily read standard road signs
  • gets lost or confused on familiar roads
  • notices other drivers often honking
  • hears concern from family, friends or police

There may be a middle step. The DMV suggests driving in daylight only, avoiding rush hour, sticking to familiar roads, taking shorter trips and using roads with lower speed limits. It also recommends a behind-the-wheel evaluation by a driver rehabilitation specialist, often an occupational therapist at a hospital or clinic. Health insurance normally pays for that evaluation if the person has a medical diagnosis and a doctor's referral, so check the plan. The therapist doesn't report results to the DMV without the driver's written consent.

Ask about medicines and eyes first

The DMV notes that many medicines, even over the counter, can impair driving, and that cataracts and other vision problems can quickly affect it. New glasses or a medicine change sometimes solve the problem. Ask the doctor or pharmacist for a review.

How do you talk with a parent about giving up the keys?

Start early, keep it about safety and independence, and come with a plan for getting around. The DMV says a license is often a symbol of independence, and that stopping after many years is a big adjustment.

  • Pick a calm moment. Not right after a scare, and not in front of others.
  • Use specifics. Name what you saw, like a missed stop sign on a familiar road.
  • Bring in the doctor. A doctor or a driving evaluation can give a neutral opinion.
  • Have rides lined up. Map out how your parent will get to the grocery store, doctor, place of worship and friends.
  • Swap the license for an ID. The DMV lets drivers exchange a license, current or expired within two years, for a non-driver photo ID that serves the same identification purpose. Apply by mail or at a DMV office.

What are the other ways to get around?

  • Reduced fare transit. Riders 65 and older pay half fare on MTA subways and buses. See our MTA reduced fare guide, which also covers some upstate systems.
  • Paratransit. In NYC, people whose disability keeps them off buses and subways may qualify for Access-A-Ride shared rides. See our Access-A-Ride guide.
  • County senior rides. Many county Offices for the Aging offer or point to senior rides. In Suffolk, for example, the towns run senior transportation, with medical appointments given priority. Find the number on your county page, such as Rockland, Westchester or Orange.
  • Senior center rides. Some senior centers provide transportation. See our senior centers guide.

If you aren't sure where to start, NY Connects at 1-800-342-9871 can point you to local transportation, and our caregiver support guide covers help for families.

faq.q: How do I report my dad's unsafe driving to the DMV in Westchester?
faq.a: Fill out DMV form DS-7, Request for Driver Review, with specific incidents, dates and places, sign it, and mail the original to Medical Review Unit, NYS DMV, 6 Empire State Plaza, Room 337, Albany, NY 12228. The DMV does not take reports by phone or email, and your name and signature are required.

faq.q: Does my mom in Staten Island need a road test to renew her license?
faq.a: No. New York has no age-based road test. She needs to pass a vision test, with at least 20/40 in one or both eyes, with or without glasses. She can test at a DMV office or with a Vision Registry provider, then renew online, by mail or in person.

faq.q: At what age do you have to stop driving in New York?
faq.a: There is no set age. The DMV says it will not remove driving privileges based on age or any standard except driving ability. A driver can be re-evaluated when the DMV gets a specific report from a doctor, police officer or someone who knows the driver.

faq.q: How much is the defensive driving discount in New York?
faq.a: Completing a DMV-approved Point and Insurance Reduction Program course reduces the base rate of auto insurance premiums by 10% each year for three years. Take it once every 36 months to keep the discount. Only the principal operator on a policy gets the reduction.

faq.q: Will the DMV tell my parent who reported them?
faq.a: The DS-7 form requires your name, signature and relationship to the driver, and the DMV may contact you. At the interview, the examiner explains the information that was received and lets the driver respond. Ask the DMV about confidentiality before you file.

faq.q: What can my parent use as ID after giving up driving?
faq.a: A New York State non-driver photo ID. The DMV lets drivers exchange a current license, or one that expired within the last two years, for a non-driver ID by mail or at a DMV office. It provides the same proof of identification as a driver license.

title: Senior centers in New York: meals, classes and how to find one
seoTitle: Senior Centers in New York: Meals, Classes, How to Join
seoDesc: New York senior centers are open to anyone 60+. Free NYC older adult centers, county meal sites, suggested contributions and how to find one near you.
dek: Anyone 60 or older in New York can join a senior center for lunch, classes and company, with no income test. Here is what centers offer, what meals cost and how to find one in your county or borough.
keyFacts: Community dining is open to anyone 60+, with no income test
Meals are free; a voluntary contribution is suggested
NYC has more than 300 older adult centers and affiliated sites
Meals are served at about 1,000 locations across New York State
body:
Senior centers in New York are open to anyone 60 or older, and you do not need to show your income to join. They serve a hot lunch on weekdays, run classes and exercise programs, and have staff who help members sign up for benefits.

In New York City they are called older adult centers (OACs), funded by NYC Aging, and membership is free. Everywhere else, your county Office for the Aging runs or funds senior centers and community dining sites, where lunch costs nothing but you are invited to give a small, voluntary contribution. This guide covers what centers offer, what the meals cost, and how to find one in your county or borough.

What does a senior center in New York offer?

Most centers offer a nutritious midday meal, social activities, classes, fitness programs and help with benefits. The exact mix depends on the center, so call the one near you for its schedule.

NYC Aging says its more than 300 older adult centers and affiliated sites across the five boroughs provide healthy meals, activities, classes, fitness programs and social services. The classes and activities it lists include:

  • Arts and crafts, music and theater arts
  • Computer classes
  • Dominos, bingo, chess and ping-pong
  • Gardening
  • Recreational day trips
  • Holiday and birthday celebrations

For health, NYC Aging lists walking clubs, yoga, chair exercises, tai chi, dance and Zumba, plus chronic disease self-management classes for people with arthritis, diabetes and high blood pressure, and falls prevention workshops. Staff also help members with benefits such as Medicare and Medicaid, the rent freeze program (SCRIE) and SNAP. On-site and virtual mental health services are offered at over 80 centers through NYC Aging's Mental Health Initiative.

Outside the city, county programs look similar. Westchester County says many of its congregate dining centers add social and educational activities such as exercise programs, dance, arts and crafts, health promotion and outings. Suffolk County describes its congregate programs as a nutritious midday meal plus a chance for socialization and recreation, often with seminars too.

You do not need to be lonely, low-income or frail to walk in. If you are 60, the door is open.

Who can go, and what does lunch cost?

Anyone 60 or older can eat at a community dining site in New York, and it is not an income-based program. The New York State Office for the Aging (NYSOFA) says there is no charge for the meals, but each person is offered the chance to make a suggested voluntary contribution.

A few family members can come too. According to NYSOFA:

  • A spouse can get meals even if he or she is under 60.
  • A person with a disability younger than 60 who lives with an older adult may use the dining site.
  • At a dining site inside housing mainly for older adults, residents with disabilities may also get meals.

State rules protect people who can't pay. NYSOFA's contribution policy says no service can be denied or affected by a person's inability or unwillingness to contribute, contributions are kept confidential, and a locked box must be available at group meal sites. Reminder letters or calls asking for money are not allowed, and you can't be required to show your income.

WhereWhat the official page says about cost
New York City older adult centersMembership is free for New Yorkers 60 and older
Erie County (Stay Fit Dining)$3.50 contribution suggested, not required; advance reservations required
St. Lawrence County$3 suggested voluntary contribution for people 60 and older; $5 guest fee for anyone under 60; 24-hour reservation requested
Westchester CountySmall suggested contribution, voluntary; pre-registration required
Suffolk CountyNo fee; participants are encouraged to make a voluntary contribution

How do I find an older adult center in New York City?

Call Aging Connect at 212-244-6469 (212-AGING-NY) or 311, or search the NYC Aging online service finder by address. Both can point you to the center closest to home.

Centers are run by local community organizations, and NYC Aging says centers in diverse neighborhoods serve culturally aligned meals that reflect the community. All meals are reviewed by NYC Aging nutrition staff. Some centers also serve breakfast or dinner, or offer grab-and-go meals.

NYC Aging also funds centers for specific groups, including SAGE centers and the Queens Center for Gay Seniors for LGBTQ+ older adults, and VISIONS at Selis Manor Senior Center for older adults who are blind or have low vision.

What is a NORC?

A naturally occurring retirement community (NORC) is a housing development or building that, over time, has become home to many older adults. NYC Aging says there are around 60 NORCs in the city with a social service provider on site, and it funds 36 of them. Funded NORCs offer case management, help with benefits, health care management and health promotion such as blood pressure screenings, yoga and tai chi. If your parent's building is a NORC, the services may be right downstairs.

Borough pages on this site list the local numbers: Bronx, Brooklyn, Manhattan, Queens and Staten Island.

How do I find a senior center outside New York City?

Call your county Office for the Aging, or NY Connects at 1-800-342-9871, which connects you to the local office. NYSOFA says meals are served up to five days a week at about 1,000 locations statewide, in senior centers, senior clubs, senior housing complexes, town halls and other community spots.

Some counties post their sites online. A few examples from county pages:

  • Rockland County. The Office for the Aging lists congregate meal providers, including Meals on Wheels Programs and Services of Rockland in Nanuet (845-624-6325) and the Martin Luther King Multi Purpose Center in Spring Valley (845-425-8910). Its registered dietitian, reachable at 845-364-2115, offers nutrition counseling at meal sites, at home or by phone. See the Rockland County page.
  • Westchester County. The Department of Senior Programs and Services posts a site directory, from the Fox Senior Center in Mount Kisco to the Peter Chema Senior Nutrition Center in Yonkers. Meals are served five or more days a week. See the Westchester County page.
  • Suffolk County. More than 30 nutrition programs. Call 631-853-8227 to find one. The county says many of its nutrition programs provide transportation. See the Suffolk County page.
  • Erie County. Stay Fit Dining serves weekday noon meals at senior centers across the county. To register, call the site nearest you. For food worries, call NY Connects at 716-858-8526. See the Erie County page.

Many towns also run their own senior centers and clubs. Our town pages list senior centers town by town, and every county page lists the Office for the Aging number.

  1. Find the office. Open your parent's county page on this site, or call NY Connects at 1-800-342-9871. In the five boroughs, call 212-244-6469 or 311.
  2. Ask for the closest sites. Ask which senior centers or dining sites are nearest, which days they serve lunch, and whether any offer rides.
  3. Reserve the meal. Many counties require a reservation, sometimes a day ahead. Erie, Westchester and St. Lawrence all say so.
  4. Ask for the calendar. Request the monthly activity schedule and menu so you can pick a good first day, like a class or celebration.
  5. Go together the first time. A first visit is easier with company. Introduce your parent to the site manager and ask about special diets.
  6. Ask about other help. Staff can often help with SNAP, Medicare, Medicaid and more. Bring questions.

Can a senior center help if my parent can't get there?

Yes, in two ways. Some centers provide rides, and people who can't shop or cook may qualify for home-delivered meals.

NYSOFA says some community sites provide transportation for people who need help getting to a meal location. In New York City, NYC Aging says some centers offer transportation to essential medical and social service appointments. Reduced-fare transit can also help; see our MTA reduced fare guide and Access-A-Ride guide.

NYSOFA says home-delivered meals are for older New Yorkers who can't prepare meals for themselves, for example after a hospital stay. Unlike lunch at a center, they require an interview with the local office to see if your parent qualifies. That same interview can turn up other services, such as in-home help through EISEP. Start with NY Connects.

Food help beyond lunch

NYSOFA's Senior Farmers' Market Nutrition Program gives eligible low-income adults 60 and older $25 in coupons once a year for fresh produce at participating farmers' markets. Booklets come out in July, can be used through November and go first come, first served. Ask the Office for the Aging or the center. For grocery money, see our SNAP guide.

What should families know before the first visit?

Expect a mix of regulars and newcomers, and a set lunch time. Call ahead, because schedules, menus and services differ from center to center.

  • Lunch is usually around midday. Erie County serves at noon. St. Lawrence County sites list 11:30 a.m. Arrive a little early.
  • Special diets. In Westchester, for example, menus are planned by a registered dietitian nutritionist. Ask what the center can do for diabetic, low-sodium or kosher needs before you go.
  • Nutrition counseling. NYSOFA says registered dietitians offer private counseling on diabetes, weight and healthy eating, and you don't have to eat the meals to meet with one.
  • Volunteering counts. Some older adults start by helping at the meal site or driving meals. NYSOFA says local programs rely on volunteers.
  • A slow start is fine. If your dad doesn't like the first visit, try a different day or another center. Activities change week to week.

What mistakes should you avoid?

  • Assuming it costs money. Contributions are voluntary. No one should be turned away for not paying.
  • Showing up without a reservation. Many counties need a day's notice to plan meals.
  • Calling the wrong office. In the five boroughs it is NYC Aging. Elsewhere it is the county Office for the Aging.
  • Stopping at lunch. Center staff often know about local rides, legal help, caregiver programs and benefits. Ask.

If you care for a parent and need a break, our caregiver support guide covers respite and support groups, and our free and discounted guide lists other ways to save.

faq.q: How do I find a senior center for my mom in Queens?
faq.a: Call Aging Connect at 212-244-6469 or 311, or use the NYC Aging service finder online and enter her address. Older adult center membership is free for New Yorkers 60 and older. Ask the center for its monthly calendar and whether it serves breakfast, dinner or grab-and-go meals.

faq.q: Is there a senior lunch program near my dad in Rockland County?
faq.a: Yes. The Rockland County Office for the Aging lists congregate meal providers including Meals on Wheels Programs and Services of Rockland in Nanuet (845-624-6325) and the Martin Luther King Multi Purpose Center in Spring Valley (845-425-8910). Call ahead to register and ask about lunch days.

faq.q: Do you have to pay for lunch at a New York senior center?
faq.a: No. NYSOFA says there is no charge for congregate meals. You are offered a chance to make a suggested voluntary contribution, such as $3.50 in Erie County or $3 in St. Lawrence County. Contributions are confidential and no one can be denied a meal for not giving.

faq.q: Can my spouse come to a senior center if they are under 60?
faq.a: Yes, for meals. NYSOFA says a spouse can get meals at a community dining site even if they are under 60. A person with a disability under 60 who lives with an older adult may use the site too. Some counties, such as St. Lawrence, charge a guest fee to other people under 60.

faq.q: Do I need a reservation to eat at a senior meal site?
faq.a: Often, yes. Erie County requires advance reservations, Westchester County requires pre-registration, and St. Lawrence County asks for 24 hours' notice. Call the site or your county Office for the Aging before the first visit.

faq.q: What if my parent can't get to a senior center?
faq.a: Ask about rides, since some sites provide transportation. If your parent can't prepare meals, they may qualify for home-delivered meals after an interview with the county Office for the Aging or NYC Aging. Call NY Connects at 1-800-342-9871 to start.
